doc.title: Sam Kininger interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 27, 2011

chapter: Boston, Berklee and the band family
title: A hard life: vans, floors and having other options
summary: Not rich; touring in vans, sharing rooms and scraping by; value of extra skills like production.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: Nice. Is it a hard life?
Yeah. It is. I mean you’re not going to make a million dollars. You know what I mean?
Yeah. It’s like an oxymoron, rich jazz musician.
I think people don’t realize that.
They probably see you up on stage.

I know. Like all these people and you think it’s — but man a lot of it throughout the years, you know, packed in the van with the whole band, and then carrying stuff in and out. People don’t see all the sharing hotel rooms and sleeping on the floor in sleeping bags and just scraping by just to make even you know. And then if there was any left and we got lucky we got paid, most of the time. But it’s one of those, you know, you can stick it out or try something else I guess.

The people that don’t stick it out and try something else, do you think that they have more options? Like well I was good at accounting. Or I could be an accountant as well as a musician so, I don’t know if I really asked that question but —

Like having more options is definitely a better thing. I would say even as a musician going to school for maybe not performance but adding something to it like production engineering so that you have another outlet as far as being in the scene but so that you don’t have to be an accountant or something else. You know what I mean?
